submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole is a retrospective lexical detector for the predicate vocabulary of technical and clinical claims, and it answers to word-forms rather than to meanings or register. (1) In any register and any syntactic role it fires on the intervention verbs and their inflections - cause(s/d/ing), prevent(s/ed/ing), stop(s/ped/ping), halt(ed), cure(s/d), treat(ed/ing), protect(s/ed), affect(s/ed), infect(s/ed), block(s/ed), inhibit(s/ed), suppress(es/ed), eliminate(s/d), kill(s/ed), mitigate(s/d), alleviate(s/d), reduce(s/d) - on the relational adjectives that grade a thing against a standard or an agent - resistant, susceptible, vulnerable, liable, tolerant, allergic, compatible, valid, identical, comparable, equivalent, similar, related, associated, stable, serious, minimal, worth, able, close - and on the nominals quality, detection, sensitivity and mechanism: 'a good cause', 'treated his guests to dinner', 'the old clock stopped' and 'the shop is close' fire as strongly as a journal sentence, so register and part of speech are not part of the feature. (2) Only inside technical or clinical prose does the same lift reach the further change- and method-words removed, returned, recovered, processed, sequenced, assayed, effective, reliable and consistent, which stay near its floor in a narrative sentence with the same word. (3) Everywhere it stays below 0.35 for entity nouns (protein, tissue, hospital, committee), for absolute harm and severity adjectives (harmful, toxic, dangerous, sensitive, prone, immune, chronic, acute, mild, significant) and for narrative or plain-reporting verbs (walked, talked, played, made, gave, used, said, started, ended, continued, spread, persisted, failed, improved, increased, declined, changed, measured, tested, observed, reported, monitored, analysed, assessed, examined, described). Peaks run 0.9-2.2 in a plain sentence and 1.5-3.2 when the trigger is the predicate of a that/which relative clause, and a probe's strength is the maximum over its tokens, so one trigger anywhere in the sentence carries it. The pole's output lens is incoherent (whitespace tokens under the Jacobian lens, 0% logit/Jacobian agreement, kurtosis 99.6), so no upcoming-token set is claimed.

rival_explanations: The pole is a register detector rather than a lexical one: it fires on any content word of technical or clinical prose (it should fire on 'measured', 'tested', 'collected', 'removed', 'amount', 'processed' in a lab sentence and stay quiet in an everyday one), so the listed words are only the densest part of a general technical-style effect.

Only the causal and clinical verb core fires - cause, prevent, stop, treat, cure, halt, protect and resistant - and the relational adjectives and nominals (identical, similar, comparable, valid, related, quality, detection, mechanism) are incidental co-activations that would not survive a fresh sample, so a probe built on those words should be quiet.

The pole tracks the syntax of a subordinate clause rather than the word: it fires on the finite predicate of a that/which relative clause or a copular predicate whatever the verb, so 'the treatment that failed', 'the strain that persisted' and 'the method was simple' should fire while the same words in a main clause stay at the floor.

From National Geographic News:
Five foot long tracks of a six-legged water scorpion reveal that Hibbertopterus could have lumbered along the riverbanks of Scotland 330 million years ago,
Illo © Nature 2005
"There's been lot of debate about this particular [species of] water scorpion—whether it could only live in water or if it could come out. What the track shows is they could come out at least for short intervals," Martin Whyte, a geologist at the University of Sheffield in England said.
The track itself is 20 feet (6 meters) long and about 3 feet (1 meter) wide. The creature walked in-phase, with each pair of limbs moving forward at the same time rather than alternating, like a human gait. Also, the scorpion's stride averaged 10.6 inches (27 centimeters) long, short enough that they overlapped. The track also features a central groove left by the water scorpion's dragging tail, leaving indications of jerky movements.
"The whole thing adds up to fairly look as though the body [was] heavy and the animal was moving quite slowly," Whyte said. "For that reason I think it was out of the water. Had it been in [the water], water would've buoyed up the tail."
By about 360 million years ago the transition of lobe-finned fish—prehistoric fish with fleshy fins—to four-limbed tetrapods was nearly complete. The newly discovered trackway, which is dated to 330 million years ago, therefore suggests that some of the earliest tetrapods would have confronted these giant water scorpions as they scurried about the shore.

The video opens with a close-up shot of a great white shark paddling solo in the middle of a turquoise ocean, but when it zooms out, the camera reveals the bustling coast of a Southern California beach.
"You are paddleboarding next to approximately 15 great white sharks," comes a voice from the local Sheriff's Department. "The sharks are as close as the surfline."
The voice belonged to Orange County Sheriff's Department Deputy Brian Stockbridge, who on Wednesday advised a group of paddle-boarders at Capistrano Beach to "exit the water in a calm manner," according to The Orange County Register.
The area where the sharks were seen, which is located south of California's San Onofre State Beach, was the same spot where last month a woman suffered a shark bite. The area was also put under shark advisory, according to an announcement by Camp Pendleton.
But while it might seem like sharks are becoming more and more of a threat, experts say the opposite scenario is closer to the truth.
"We may never know exactly how many sharks are out there, or exactly how many are killed each year. What we do know, from a variety of different types of analysis, is that many species of sharks are decreasing in population at alarming rates," writes University of Miami marine biologist David Shiffman.
One frequently-cited survey of data published in 2003 from fisheries gathered between 1986 and 2000 suggests that shark populations are in deep trouble.
The data from that survey found that hammerhead populations were declining by an average of 89%; great whites by 79%; tiger sharks by 65%, thresher sharks by 80%, blue sharks by 60%, and mako sharks by 70%:
Sharks are the real ones in trouble
While vigilante shark hunters can do significant damage to local shark populations, the real problem centers around two main activities: Hunting sharks for their meat and fins and irresponsible fishing practices. Each year, thousands of sharks are caught and trapped in fishing nets and other fishing gear.
And while it might seem like good news that there are fewer sharks around, it's actually a very big problem for the rest of us.
In many places, sharks are apex predators, meaning they occupy the spot right at the top of the food chain. If their populations aren't healthy and stable, it throws all of the other life in the oceans out of balance.
Plus, sharks have a bunch of characteristics that make them especially vulnerable to exploitation, including the fact that they live long lives, mature late in life, and have very few young.

The way the Northern Light or aurora works is a lot like a neon sign, except that in the aurorae the conducting gas is in the ionosphere, instead of a glass tube, and the current travels along magnetic field lines instead of copper wires.
The power source for aurorae is Solar Wind. The Earth's magnetic field looks a lot like the magnetic field of a bar magnet with field lines going into and out of the Earth's magnetic poles, where the magnetic field is strongest. Solar Wind from the Sun is always pushing on the Earth's magnetic field (the magnetosphere), deforming and stretching it into a long leeward tail like the wake of a ship, which is called the magnetotail The aurora happens when energetic particles (protons and electrons) from the Sun enter the Earth's magnetosphere and are captured in the magnetotail. When disturbances occur in the Solar Wind or there is an energetic Solar Flare, the particles are accelerated along the field lines, becoming more dense near the magnetic poles and eventually precipitating into the Earth's ionosphere. As they hit the ionosphere the particles will inevitably collide violently with gas atoms. This adds energy to the gas atoms which in turn will release light and more elec trons - the ionosphere starts to glow!
The different colours in an aurora are depending on the distribution of different gases at different altitudes. Very high in the ionosphere (above 300km) oxygen is the most common gas resulting in reddish colours when exited. Other gases like nitrogene and helium produce blue or purple colours.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The committee walked through the hospital corridor and talked about the new tissue samples.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Entity nouns (committee, hospital, tissue) and narrative verbs (walked, talked) in a clinical setting; the hypothesis puts every one of these below 0.35.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The technicians measured the amount of protein in each sample and collected the results in a spreadsheet.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Lab prose holding only plain-reporting verbs and entity nouns that the hypothesis lists as floor-level, so it tests whether technical register alone is enough.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The guard was sensitive about his accent and would not talk to the visitors from the north.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'sensitive' is the severity adjective the hypothesis names as a floor item, a near-miss of the trigger nominal 'sensitivity'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Her skin was sensitive to the cream, and the nurse wrote the reaction in the chart.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Medical context plus 'sensitive', which the hypothesis explicitly keeps below 0.35, separating clinical topic from the lexical claim.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The fumes in the garage were dangerous and toxic, so we kept the children indoors and aired the room.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Absolute harm adjectives (dangerous, toxic) are on the hypothesis's floor list even though they carry the same claim of harm as 'cause'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The change was mild and hardly significant, so the committee continued as before.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Severity adjectives and the plain-reporting verb 'continued' that the hypothesis lists as inactive, a paraphrase of the harm vocabulary without a trigger.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The rumour spread through the village, and the old quarrel persisted for many years.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Narrative continuation verbs (spread, persisted) are named floor items, testing that the pole is not a general 'persistence' detector.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The method that failed had been tested twice, and the report described it as safe.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A that-relative clause over a non-trigger predicate with plain-reporting verbs, inactive under the hypothesis but predicted active by the clause-syntax rival.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The result was simple and the sample looked clean, though the lab reported no problems.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Lab report with only entity nouns, copular adjectives and 'reported', all on the hypothesis's floor list.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The parcel returned to the sender, and the shop processed the refund without a word.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The clause-2 change-words 'returned' and 'processed' in a narrative sentence, where the hypothesis says they stay near the floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The effect of the noise on the class was small, and the teacher changed the seating plan.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The noun 'effect' is a near-miss of the claimed trigger 'affect'; the hypothesis says only the verb forms count.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He walked to the shop, talked to the clerk, and made a small joke about the weather.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Plain-reporting verbs (walked, talked, made) in an everyday sentence, every one a listed floor item.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The old vase was fragile, and we wrapped it in newspaper before the move.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'fragile' carries the vulnerability sense of the claimed trigger 'vulnerable' but is not one of the claimed word-forms, so the lexical hypothesis predicts the floor for this copular everyday sentence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The team observed the mice for weeks, monitored their weight, and reported the findings.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A research report whose only verbs are the plain-reporting verbs the hypothesis calls inactive, checking that technical topic is not enough.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The bridge collapsed after the storm, and engineers examined the wreckage for hours.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Engineering prose with no trigger, only the listed floor verb 'examined', testing technical register without the claimed vocabulary.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The choir played the old songs and the audience gave them loud applause.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Narrative verbs 'played' and 'gave' that the hypothesis keeps below 0.35.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The witness described the car and said it had turned left at the lights.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Plain-reporting verbs 'described' and 'said', both on the floor list.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The patient had a chronic cough and an acute fever, and the doctor noted mild dehydration.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Clinical prose holding only severity adjectives (chronic, acute, mild) that the hypothesis explicitly excludes, a hard near-miss for a clinical-word detector.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The child was prone to colds and immune to the usual remedies, the parents said.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'prone' and 'immune' are the vulnerability adjectives the hypothesis separates from its triggers, in reported everyday speech.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The committee reviewed the budget and continued the discussion into the afternoon.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Plain-reporting verbs 'reviewed' and 'continued', listed floor items with no trigger.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: A good cause can still attract volunteers, and the fair raised money for the library roof.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The hypothesis says the noun 'cause' in a narrative clause fires as strongly as a journal sentence; this is the civic-fundraising sense it cites.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She treated his guests to dinner and then talked about the harvest until midnight.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The hospitality sense of 'treated' that the hypothesis names as a should-fire case, testing that meaning is not part of the feature.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The old clock stopped in the night, and nobody noticed until the morning.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The hypothesis's own example 'the old clock stopped', a non-clinical intransitive use.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They stopped the car at the edge of town and unloaded the bags from the boot.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A main-clause trigger with no relative clause or copula, active under the hypothesis but at the floor for the clause-syntax rival.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The two copies were similar in every way, and the price seemed worth the trip.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Relational adjectives 'similar' and 'worth' in an everyday comparison, claimed to fire regardless of register and which the core-verb rival treats as incidental.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The alloy is compatible with the new sealant, and the lab expects the joint to hold.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'compatible' is a claimed relational adjective in a materials-science context unlike the clinical examples.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The detection of the fault took months, and the lab's mechanism for logging complaints was slow.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed nominals 'detection' and 'mechanism' in a technical sentence with no verb trigger.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Doctors say the drug can halt the growth of the tumour in most cases.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'halt' is a claimed verb form not seen in the top examples, in a clinical register.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The knight's shield was resistant to the blade, and the crowd cheered from the stands.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A cross-genre holdout: 'resistant' in fantasy narrative, which the hypothesis says fires because register is not part of the feature.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The samples were returned to the lab, processed within an hour, and sequenced overnight.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Clause-2 change- and method-words 'returned', 'processed' and 'sequenced' inside technical prose, where the hypothesis says they lift.
